rows.subtype: Approach: understanding parental worries first [Thinking]
rows.description: The teenager asks why parents refuse late evenings out and learns the concerns are safety and late-night travel, not distrust, which allows a plan that addresses those specific concerns.

rows.subtype: Approach: win-win proposal with conditions [Action]
rows.description: The teen proposes going to a friend's house until 8 pm, sharing the address and location, phoning on arrival and being picked up by a parent, offering a trial for a month.

rows.subtype: Approach: demanding and arguing [Pitfall]
rows.description: The teen shouts that everyone else is allowed and that parents are too strict. The argument turns into a power struggle, parents dig in and the request for freedom is refused outright.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing after a broken agreement [Revision]
rows.description: After coming home late once, the teen owns up, explains the reason without excuses and proposes a stricter check-in for two weeks, showing that trust can be repaired rather than lost.

rows.subtype: Approach: finishing homework first, then playing [Action]
rows.description: A boy makes a rule that games start only after homework, and finds that with work done he enjoys the game more without worry in the back of his mind.

rows.subtype: Approach: time-boxing game sessions [Action]
rows.description: A girl sets a timer for forty minutes of gaming on weekdays, and when it rings she stops, making the limit feel like her own rule rather than a parent's.

rows.subtype: Approach: just one more level [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child tells himself only one more round, then another, and suddenly it is ten p.m. with unfinished maths, showing how a fun activity without a stopping point expands.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing tiredness and changing the routine [Revision]
rows.description: After falling asleep in class from late gaming, the boy realises the cost, moves gaming to the afternoon and puts the console away by nine at night.

rows.subtype: Approach: acts quickly when time is short and the situation is urgent [Thinking]
rows.description: A student sees a friend faint at a hostel event and acts at once, calling for help, since there is no time for a detailed plan.

rows.subtype: Approach: takes time and sleeps on it when the decision is slow and important [Thinking]
rows.description: A student weighing whether to pursue further study lets the decision take a month, gathering facts and talking to family, since no deadline forces speed.

rows.subtype: Approach: uses one method for every problem out of habit [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student who likes detailed timetables uses them even for creative work, where a loose start would suit better, and feels blocked.

rows.subtype: Approach: pausing and recognising pressure tactics [Thinking]
rows.description: A teen gets a call saying his father's account will be blocked in ten minutes unless an OTP is shared, notices the urgency and fear, and treats the pressure itself as the warning sign.

rows.subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of scam scripts [Thinking]
rows.description: After reading examples of common frauds, a teen rehearses aloud what she would say to a fake officer or a fake job offer, so a calm refusal is ready when a real call arrives.

rows.subtype: Approach: trusting a caller who knows some personal details [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student believes a caller because he knows her school name and her father's name, not realising such details are easily collected, and starts sharing more information to be helpful.

rows.subtype: Approach: containing the damage after a slip [Revision]
rows.description: Realising he entered his login on a fake page, a student changes the password at once, logs out other devices, turns on two-step verification, and tells a parent so the bank can be warned.

rows.subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
rows.subtype: Approach: list all demands and rank them by urgency and importance [Thinking]
rows.description: A final-year student lists hospital visits, exams, assignments and household tasks, and decides that treatment appointments and the coming exam are the top priorities. Ranking gives a way to say no to the rest.

rows.subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
rows.subtype: Approach: share the care schedule with siblings and relatives [Action]
rows.description: The student writes a weekly rota for hospital stays, medicine pickup and cooking and asks a sibling, an aunt and a neighbour to take fixed slots. Sharing the care prevents burnout of one person.

rows.subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
rows.subtype: Approach: take on everything alone to prove devotion [Pitfall]
rows.description: Feeling that asking for help is disloyal, the student does every task and sleeps four hours. Exhaustion leads to a failed test and short temper, which makes the care worse.

rows.subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
rows.subtype: Approach: notice signs of caregiver fatigue and step back [Revision]
rows.description: Realising that irritation and poor sleep are constant, the student asks an aunt to take two nights and books a counselling session. Recognising limits keeps the care sustainable.

rows.subtype: Approach: bargaining [Action]
rows.description: A child swaps the toy truck for a turn with the friend's doll. Both get something they want, so the trade feels fair to both.

rows.subtype: Approach: if-then rule [Thinking]
rows.description: A child reasons, "If I share the truck, then Aarav shares his cars." The rule ties giving to getting, and makes it less costly to hand the toy over.

rows.subtype: Approach: magical thinking [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child fears that the toy will be "used up" or will change once a friend touches it, and hides it. The fear has no basis but decides what the child does.

rows.subtype: Approach: asking an adult [Revision]
rows.description: Two children pull on one toy until a teacher is asked, and she proposes a sand timer for each turn. The child follows the rule the timer sets.
